paragraphs: 1,2-Dichlorobenzene (CASRN: 95-50-1; DTXSID: DTXSID6020430; PubChem CID: 7239; EC Number: 202-425-9) is a chlorinated aromatic hydrocarbon with the molecular formula C₆H₄Cl₂ and a molecular weight of 147.0 g/mol [1]. It is produced industrially by the chlorination of benzene or monochlorobenzene in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst, or alternatively via the Sandmeyer procedure from the appropriate chloroaniline precursor; these processes yield mixtures of ortho-, meta-, and para-dichlorobenzene isomers, which are subsequently separated [2]. The compound serves as a chemical intermediate in the synthesis of 3,4-dichloroaniline, dyes, herbicides, and pharmaceuticals, and functions as a solvent, heat transfer liquid, degreasing agent, paint solvent, paint remover, cylinder lubricant, and a solvent for waxes, gums, resins, tars, rubber, oils, and asphalts [2]. It is also employed as a deodorant and, historically, as an insecticide and soil fumigant, although its pesticide registrations in the United States have been cancelled and no currently registered pesticide products contain this substance [2]. Industrial products incorporating 1,2-dichlorobenzene include metal degreasing formulations and paint solvent preparations [2]. Consumer products have included deodorizers and cleaning agents. Technical-grade material typically contains 70–85% of the ortho-isomer, with the remainder consisting of meta- and para-dichlorobenzene isomers, trace chlorobenzene, and trichlorobenzene; pure-grade material contains greater than 99.8% of the ortho-isomer [2]. Human exposure may occur in occupational settings among chemical manufacturing plant operators, metal degreasing workers, paint formulators, and laboratory personnel through inhalation of vapors and dermal contact with the liquid [2]. Residential and consumer exposure may arise from the use of products containing the compound in enclosed spaces. Environmental exposure pathways include volatilization from industrial waste streams into ambient air, leaching from contaminated soil into groundwater, and adsorption to sediments in surface water bodies receiving industrial effluents [2].

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) has established a permissible exposure limit (PEL) for 1,2-dichlorobenzene of 50 ppm (300 mg/m³) as a ceiling value under Table Z-1 [4]. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has established a recommended exposure limit (REL) of 50 ppm (300 mg/m³) as a 15-minute ceiling value [5]. Authoritative threshold limit value (TLV) documentation from the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) was not available for review at the time of this writing; the relevant ACGIH documentation requires a subscription and specific values could not be confirmed from the data sources consulted [2]. No maximum contaminant level (MCL) or maximum contaminant level goal (MCLG) under the Safe Drinking Water Act has been identified for 1,2-dichlorobenzene in the data sources reviewed for this report [3]. The EPA Integrated Risk Information System (IRIS) assessment for 1,2-dichlorobenzene was not accessible at the time of this writing due to a system error; accordingly, no oral reference dose (RfD), critical study NOAEL, or associated uncertainty factor could be confirmed from IRIS records [3]. These regulatory gaps are discussed further in the data gap analysis below.

1,2-Dichlorobenzene can be absorbed into the body by inhalation, through the skin, and by ingestion [2]. Inhalation represents the primary route of occupational exposure, given the compound's vapor pressure of 1.4 mm Hg at 25 °C, which supports meaningful volatilization under ambient conditions [2]. Following absorption, the compound is distributed to tissues throughout the body; consistent with its lipophilic character, distribution to adipose tissue and highly perfused organs, including the liver and kidneys, is anticipated [2]. Metabolism proceeds primarily via cytochrome P450-mediated oxidation, yielding reactive arene oxide intermediates and phenolic metabolites, including 3,4-dichlorophenol and 3,4-dichlorocatechol, which may be further conjugated with glucuronic acid or sulfate prior to excretion [2]. The compound has been characterized as a hepatotoxic agent, consistent with hepatic bioactivation of reactive intermediates [1]. Excretion occurs predominantly via the urine as conjugated metabolites, with a smaller fraction eliminated through exhalation as unchanged parent compound or carbon dioxide [2]. Specific quantitative half-life data were not available in the sources reviewed for this report.

The acute toxicological effects of 1,2-dichlorobenzene in humans and experimental animals include irritation of the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract following inhalation or dermal contact, as well as central nervous system depression at high exposure concentrations [2]. The compound has been identified as a hepatotoxic agent, and liver injury represents a principal target organ effect observed in experimental animal studies [1][2]. Subchronic toxicity data characterizing effects following repeated intermediate-duration exposures were not available in the sources reviewed for this report; this represents a recognized gap in the hazard characterization database, as discussed below. Chronic toxicity data sufficient to characterize lifetime health risks from prolonged exposure were similarly not available from the sources consulted [2][3]. With respect to carcinogenicity, no authoritative cancer weight-of-evidence classification from the U.S. EPA, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), or other regulatory bodies was identified in the data sources reviewed for this report [3]. The absence of a cancer classification precludes a definitive characterization of the carcinogenic potential of 1,2-dichlorobenzene at this time.

The mechanism of toxicity of 1,2-dichlorobenzene is understood to involve cytochrome P450-mediated bioactivation to reactive arene oxide intermediates, which may covalently bind to cellular macromolecules, including proteins and DNA, thereby initiating cytotoxic and potentially genotoxic events [2]. Oxidative stress resulting from the generation of reactive oxygen species during metabolic activation is considered a contributing mechanism, particularly in the liver, where bioactivation is most active [2]. The phenolic and catechol metabolites produced during oxidative metabolism may undergo further redox cycling, amplifying oxidative damage to hepatic and renal tissues [2]. Glutathione depletion has been proposed as a secondary mechanism by which reactive intermediates overwhelm cellular antioxidant defenses, leading to lipid peroxidation and cell death [2]. The specific molecular targets and signaling pathways perturbed by 1,2-dichlorobenzene at toxicologically relevant doses have not been fully elucidated, and the genomic dose-response relationships underlying these mechanisms remain incompletely characterized, providing a principal scientific rationale for the present study.

A review of available regulatory and toxicological databases reveals several significant gaps in the hazard characterization and risk assessment of 1,2-dichlorobenzene. In the domain of hazard identification, subchronic toxicity data characterizing effects following repeated intermediate-duration exposures are absent from the sources reviewed, representing a gap relevant to the assessment of occupational and repeated consumer exposure scenarios [2][3]. Chronic toxicity data sufficient to support characterization of lifetime health risks are likewise unavailable, precluding a complete assessment of long-term exposure consequences [3]. No authoritative cancer classification has been identified from EPA, IARC, or other bodies, leaving the carcinogenic potential of 1,2-dichlorobenzene uncharacterized and preventing a weight-of-evidence determination [3]. In the domain of dose-response assessment, no oral reference dose (RfD) was confirmed from IRIS records due to a system access error at the time of this writing; without an established RfD, NOAEL, or point of departure from a critical study, health-based oral exposure limits and drinking water guidelines cannot be derived from first principles, and benchmark dose modeling or read-across from structurally related dichlorobenzene isomers may be required as interim approaches [3]. In the domain of risk characterization, no drinking water MCL or MCLG has been identified for 1,2-dichlorobenzene, meaning that environmental contamination of drinking water sources cannot be evaluated against an enforceable federal standard [3]. By contrast, exposure characterization is relatively well-supported: occupational exposure limits (OSHA PEL and NIOSH REL) are established [4][5], industrial and consumer uses are documented [2], and environmental fate and transport data are available [2]. Absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) data are also available at a qualitative level from the ATSDR Toxicological Profile, though quantitative pharmacokinetic parameters are incompletely characterized [2]. The ATSDR Toxicological Profile and the EPA IRIS assessment represent key reference documents for this chemical; the IRIS assessment was inaccessible at the time of this writing, and the ATSDR ToxProfile text was not fully retrievable, limiting the depth of the hazard characterization presented herein.

Given the widespread industrial and historical consumer uses of 1,2-dichlorobenzene, its potential for occupational and environmental human exposure via inhalation, dermal contact, and ingestion, its established hepatotoxicity and proposed mechanism of bioactivation-mediated oxidative stress, and the identified gaps in subchronic and chronic toxicity data, cancer classification, oral dose-response characterization, and drinking water standards, this 5-day genomic dose-response study was conducted to characterize concentration-dependent gene expression changes in relevant biological pathways, identify molecular targets and mechanisms of toxicity at the transcriptomic level, and generate data that may inform point-of-departure derivation and support a more complete hazard characterization for this chemical.

text.heading: The sentences distilled from it for the Abstract
paragraphs: 1,2-Dichlorobenzene (1,2-DCB) is a member of the chlorinated aromatic hydrocarbon class of compounds to which humans may be exposed occupationally via inhalation and dermal contact during chemical manufacturing, metal degreasing, and paint formulation, and environmentally through volatilization from industrial waste streams, contaminated groundwater, and surface water sediments. Toxicological information on this compound is sparse, with identified gaps encompassing subchronic and chronic toxicity data, cancer classification, a confirmed oral reference dose, and drinking water standards, despite qualitative characterization of its hepatotoxicity and cytochrome P450-mediated bioactivation to reactive arene oxide intermediates.
